extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of poetry criticism; readers learning to practise close reading and practical criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for close-reading and practical criticism of poems: how to detect reading errors, evaluate form, tone, imagery, prosody, and the relation of means to ends. Emphasises diagnostic categories and common pitfalls in readers' responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of stock responses (commonplaces)
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of the stock response to hide what is actually in the poem is remarkable; commonplaces about a theme (e.g., 'Death the Leveller') may make us doubt the closeness of a reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let ready-made, conventional responses (stock reactions) substitute for attention to the poem's particularities. Examples: many readers default to familiar moral comments or clichés instead of attending to the poem's specific language and structure (see §13.12–13.13, §13.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity / felt emotion versus conventional utterance
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between genuine felt emotion and mere conventional verbal tricks; 'The poet has attempted to describe a quiet contemplative mood. He has not felt it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for 'ill‑feigned naivete' or phrases that read like a sermon or 'reach-me-down' reaction. If the emotion seems borrowed or conventional, the poem may lack sincerity and fail to convince (examples §§13.12, 13.31).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and internal consistency of imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful reading may reveal muddle where visual images conflict (e.g., references to dust, a sculptured effigy, and living cheeks that don't cohere).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If visual images are introduced 'we need, I shall maintain, at least two sets' and they must cohere; inconsistent imagery ('she is dust' then 'beautiful eyes') undermines the poem's sense and can make stanzas worthless (§13.462–13.47).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of tone to subject and intention
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge whether the poem's tone (solemn, urbane, sarcastic, didactic) fits its subject and the author's intention; misfit can create distaste or ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate how single words (e.g., 'rude') or shifts in diction alter tone; a solemn subject does not mandate solemn treatment, and tone may be conversational or ironic—determine which and evaluate success (§13.7–13.9, 13.91).

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and avoidance of clichés
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentiments that are 'by no means uncommon' or phrases that are clichéd indicate uninspired writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note when the poem 'dwells on the theme of the brevity of human life' in a vague, conventional way; clichés signal lack of genuine invention and reduce artistic value (§13.4, §13.43).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional value / does the poem impart something?
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the underlying emotion is of sufficient value to justify the reader's effort: 'the underlying emotion is not of sufficient value' renders the poem not worth attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poem should offer feeling or insight beyond the writer 'hearing his own voice'; if it merely repeats commonplaces, it fails to reward the reader (§13.31–13.4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection and evaluation of irony or satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the poem is serious or satirical; manner may disguise seriousness by a light, artificial tone ('these words persuade the reader that the poem is not to be taken seriously').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether apparent levity masks an attack or parody; reading the poem as satire rather than solemn can radically change evaluation (see §13.45 and §13.9 discussion of a possible impish whirl).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility and appropriateness of metaphors and details
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine whether concrete details (e.g., slaves buried with a mistress in a village churchyard, exotic metaphors) are plausible or jarring in context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a metaphor or detail seems 'exotic and out of place' or culturally improbable, this may indicate faulty imagination or muddled conception, and should be questioned (§13.41–13.43, 13.46).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of reference / avoidance of ambiguous pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguities such as 'what “it” refers to?' weaken comprehension and can confuse readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pin down referents and syntactic relations; ambiguity of reference (e.g., whether 'the richest and rarest of all dowers' refers to one or several things) is a legitimate ground for criticism (§13.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre and versification regularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse syllable counts, stanzaic patterns and metrical plan; irregularities of metre can be 'very confusing and displeasing to the ear.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count lines and syllables as prosodists do; irregular metre may be a flaw unless justified by intention. Examples given in §13.61–13.63 show how stanza-to-stanza variation can displease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm and its suitability to content
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhythm should suit the poem's subject and sense; a 'tripping metre' may jar with a solemn theme, or rhetorical questions may be 'unfortunate' for a light piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test whether sense-stresses coincide with metrical ones, whether required elisions are awkward, and whether rhythmic 'lilt' supports the poem's purpose (§13.62–13.63, §13.52).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordination of means to ends (form serving content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Insist on the 'meet subordination of means to ends'—form (sound, rhythm, diction) must be subordinate to and serve the poem's purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given an interpretation of sense and emotion, judgment of form follows; misapplied form (e.g., frivolous rhythm with solemn content) indicates failure of subordination (§13.64 and surrounding discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness versus purposeful expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid dogmatic praise of conciseness; 'poetry does not aim at conciseness if there is anything to be gained by expansion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate repetition or cataloguing (e.g., 'No more she breathes, nor feels, nor stirs') for effect—what looks redundant may intentionally amplify or catalogue for artistic purposes (§13.65).

rubrics_metrics.name: Word choice and diction appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge diction for banality, pomposity, or aptness ('a phrase like “foolish pomp” is both foolish and pompous' or 'winsome personal touches strongly suggest Ella Wheeler Wilcox').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether phrasing fits the poem's voice and intention; banal or ludicrous wording undermines quality (§13.72–13.73, §13.51).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader's presuppositions and bias influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers' prior expectations (e.g., assuming solemn treatment for solemn subjects) shape their readings and can generate false critical verdicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of one's own presuppositions; many negative readings derive from a priori assumptions rather than close attention (§13.63–13.64).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing, structure and movement of the poem
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess structural unity and movement; 'structural disjointedness' or 'monstrous accosting lurch' can discomfit readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine stanzaic progression, closure and recurring patterns; abrupt or awkward structural shifts that do not serve intention are faults (§13.64).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete imagery versus symbolic ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide when images are literal (a monument, dust in eyes) and when they are symbolic; mixed modes can jar if not skillfully managed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If imagery toggles between concrete and symbolic without signposting, readers may feel muddled; supply a consistent reading or show how shifts are intentional (§13.462–13.47).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosodic technical analysis is legitimate
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical prosody (syllable counts, elision, metrical feet) is a valid part of critique: 'I am no prosodist, but those who are will doubtless have some choice comments to make.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invite or perform technical examination of versification where relevant; prosodic faults can be grounds for artistic criticism (§13.6, §13.61).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine the poet's intention before judging success
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless we know what the poet is trying to do (intention), we can hardly estimate the measure of his success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek evidence in the poem of aims (serious meditation, parody, social commentary); different intentions license different standards of success (§13.1 lead-in and §13.9 discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid applying only external measures to metre
rubrics_metrics.description: A misunderstanding of metre can derive from application of external measures; listen for internally justified rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer internal sense and stress over rigid external schemes; what sounds right within the poem's sense may differ from externally imposed counts (§13.63 commentary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdependence of functions: failure in one causes others to fail
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure of Sense, Feeling, Tone or Intention often entails aberrations in the others; 'Sometimes all four fail together... often a partial collapse of one function entails aberrations in the others.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose which function(s) fail and trace consequent effects across the poem; look for cascades of misunderstanding (§end of 'The Four Kinds of Meaning').

rubrics_metrics.name: Total Meaning is a blend of several contributory meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Language in poetry has several tasks simultaneously; Total Meaning is 'a blend, a combination of several contributory meanings of different types.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse a poem from the four aspects (Sense, Feeling, Tone, Intention) rather than seeking a single unitary meaning; weigh how these aspects combine to produce the work's effect (opening of Part Three).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense (one of the Four Kinds of Meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sense: 'We speak to say something... we use words to direct our hearers' attention upon some state of affairs, to present to them some items for consideration and to excite in them some thoughts about these items.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify what the poem asserts or describes—the propositional content or referential material—before evaluating other aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeling (one of the Four Kinds of Meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feeling: the emotional attitude toward the items referred to; 'we have an attitude towards it, some special direction, bias, or accentuation of interest... we use language to express these feelings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect and evaluate the poem's affective colouring, whether emotions are genuine and how they shape interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone (one of the Four Kinds of Meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone: the speaker's attitude to his listener; 'The tone of his utterance reflects his awareness of this relation, his sense of how he stands towards those he is addressing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine register, address, and social stance—how the poem positions itself toward its audience and how that shapes reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intention (one of the Four Kinds of Meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intention: the speaker's aim or purpose, conscious or unconscious, and the effect he is endeavouring to promote; 'Unless we know what he is trying to do, we can hardly estimate the measure of his success.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infer the poet's aims (to provoke, to console, to parody, to sermonize, etc.) and judge whether formal and rhetorical choices achieve those aims.
